findings.title: Band shares, centroid, peaks and peakShare never read the end of the file
findings.claim: mean_psd uses scipy welch with 8192-sample Hann segments at 50 % overlap. Samples after the last full segment are never read (up to 4095 samples, 85 ms at 48 kHz). The last 4096 samples before that are also weighted down to zero by the Hann taper. This is the end-of-file twin of the known start problem. lowShare, highShare, centroid, fundamental and peakShare all come from this one spectrum, and rules.py checks them (lines 83, 85, 102, 119, 123). I ran one case through rules.check and the verdict changed.
findings.evidence: A 0.5 s sound with 100 Hz hum and a 100 ms white-noise burst: burst at the start reads >4k share 0.762 (true whole-file 0.775). Burst at the end reads 0.059 (true 0.780). Centroid 971 Hz against a true 11141 Hz. A 12000-sample file, 8000 samples of 200 Hz tone then 4000 samples of noise: highShare 0.0000, lowShare 1.000, while the whole-file FFT says 22 % above 4 kHz and 73 % below 500 Hz. rules.check on a structure one-shot built like that returns [] (pass). The same samples with the noise moved to the front return ['tail-not-silent','structure-low-share','structure-high-share']. An impulse in the very last sample gives welch power 1e-39 for n = 9000, 12287 and 10000. I did not check whether any real sound in the library has loud material in its last 85 ms. Most tails are probably quiet, so the practical size of this is unknown.

findings.suggestedFix: Make every sample count equally: pad the file so the last segment ends at or after the last sample and use a window pair that sums to a constant (for example welch with boundary and padded set, or a plain Hann-windowed periodogram of the whole file for n up to a few seconds). Then decide on purpose whether the start and the end are to be weighted like the middle. No wav byte changes. Manifest numbers and some verdicts will change, so re-run the build report after the change.

findings.title: Loop level swing ignores digital silence and cannot reach 80 dB
findings.claim: levelSwingDb takes 100 ms windows (hop 50 ms) and throws away every window under -90 dB before taking max minus min. A loop that is silent for half its length therefore reads a swing of a few dB. The reported swing can never exceed (loudest window level + 90 dB). The alarm rows with swing_max=80 in cat_alarms.py (alarm_heat, alarm_missile, alarm_fuel_low, alarm_hull_critical and others) can therefore not fail unless the loudest 100 ms window is above -10 dB RMS, which is not the case for sounds levelled at -20 LUFS. Also, a loop shorter than 0.2 s returns no levelSwingDb at all, and rules.py line 80 reads that as 0.0 (pass). A loop shorter than 0.1 s skips the edge comparison and edgeOk is True.
findings.evidence: Noise 0.5 s, digital silence 1.0 s, noise 0.5 s, cuts on the 50 ms grid, 5 ms tapers: seamOk True, edgeOk True, levelSwingDb 3.5 (true: -20 dB against -inf), rules.check fails nothing, limit is 6.0. A loop dipping 110 dB: loudest window -17 dB gives 71.1, -10 dB gives 79.2, -1 dB gives 86.6, so only the last one can exceed 80. 1 s tone + 1 s digital silence reads 3.0. Noise at -20 dB for 1 s then -120 dB for 1 s reads 3.2. Pulse loops with silent gaps read about 20 dB where the true figure is unbounded. Loop of 0.15 s: levelSwingDb absent, pass True. Loop of 0.08 s: edge fields absent, pass True. In these demos the silence loops were caught only where the cut also made a seam or an edge fault. I did not check which real loops have silent windows.

findings.title: Default pyloudnorm K-weighting reads 0.04 dB low everywhere
findings.claim: pyloudnorm.Meter(sr) with the default filter class uses a generic shelf (+4 dB, 1500 Hz) and high-pass (38 Hz) approximation, not the BS.1770 coefficients. Every LUFS number is about 0.04 dB too low at 48 kHz and 44.1 kHz. filter_class='DeMan' gives the standard values. The same Meter(SR) call is also in synth/levels.py lufs(), which sets the level of every LUFS-levelled sound. The unit test allows 0.2 dB, so it cannot see this. Note on the brief's anchor: the standard gives 0.00 LKFS for a full-scale 997 Hz sine on both channels and -3.01 for one channel. The brief's -3.01 for two channels is a slip. My own independent BS.1770 code agrees with 0.00 and -3.01.
findings.evidence: 48 kHz, 997 Hz, 20 s, full scale: default one channel -3.052, two channels -0.041; DeMan one channel -3.010, two channels 0.000. 44.1 kHz: default -3.052 / -0.042; DeMan -3.008 / 0.003. Filter response against the standard prototype at 100 Hz to 20 kHz: 0.038 to 0.047 dB low at 44.1 and 48 kHz, 0.016 to 0.022 at 96 kHz. Noise 20 s: measure -13.894, reference -13.851 (48 kHz). I did not check the two-channel gating weights beyond this, and I did not look at 96 kHz files in use.

findings.title: attackMs reads 3 to 5 ms for a low steady tone that has no attack
findings.claim: The attack time is the gap between the first 1 ms peak-hold block at 10 % and the first at 90 % of the file peak. For a low-frequency tone that starts at full level, the first carrier cycle itself takes that long to rise. So a bass hum or rumble with an instant start reads a slow attack. The figure is printed for the owner and is not used by rules.py, so no verdict changes. Smaller notes: the 10 ms frame table drops the last (n mod 480) samples, so a 9 ms burst at the very end of a 1.0095 s file appears in no frame (peak frame level -120 dB; lastTenMsDb still sees it); lastTenMsDb is an RMS level, so a single-sample click of -33.2 dBFS peak in the last 10 ms reads -60.0 (rules.py checks the peak itself, so the hard rule is fine).

The same loop with gaps at -40 dB prints 40 dB and fails: the rule is inverted for the worst case. Second part: the four alarm loops are exempted with swing_max=80 (cat_alarms.py 147-151). With the drop at -90 and alarms set to about -20 LUFS, the loudest window sits about 14 dB under full scale, so the printable swing is capped near 76 dB. My sweep of beeps from 20 ms to 1 s never printed more than 74.4. The real alarm_fuel_low prints 76.3 (last manifest), the other three 9.4 to 15.1. So 80 is 3.7 dB over the worst real alarm and 65 dB over the others, and protects nothing. It is not strictly unreachable (a hotter, squarer beep could get there).
